title: Tree rings show Vikings were chopping wood in Newfoundland in 1021

cover.alt: A reconstructed Norse building at L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, with wooden plank walls and a thick roof of grass-covered sod, under a grey sky.

body: For a long time the main evidence for Vikings in America was the Icelandic sagas, stories written down centuries after the events. In 2021 a team led from the University of Groningen dated three pieces of wood from the Viking base at L’Anse aux Meadows, each from a different tree and each cut with **metal blades**, which the local Indigenous people did not make. A solar storm in 992 left a spike of radiocarbon in tree rings around the world, and in every piece that spike sat 29 rings in from the bark. So the trees were felled in **1021**, the earliest year Europeans are known to have been in the Americas, 471 years before Columbus arrived in 1492.

slides.question: In what year did Vikings cut down these trees in Newfoundland?
slides.explanation: In 1021. It is the only year of European presence in the Americas before 1492 that has been pinned down scientifically.

slides.heading: How one solar storm dated the wood

steps.label: A solar storm hits Earth in 992
Trees everywhere store a radiocarbon spike
The spike shows up in the Viking-cut wood
Count 29 rings out to the bark: 1021

slides.alt: Low grassy ridges in a green meadow outlining the walls of a Norse building at L’Anse aux Meadows, with a small information plaque in front.
slides.caption: The original buildings survive only as grassy ridges. These outline the largest Norse building at L’Anse aux Meadows, on the northern tip of Newfoundland.

left.label: The sagas
left.text: Oral stories, written down centuries later. They tell of voyages and meetings with Indigenous people, but they are contradictory and sometimes fantastical.

right.label: The tree rings
right.text: Three trees, cut with metal blades, all carrying the same solar-storm marker 29 rings from the bark. One exact year: 1021.

slides.heading: What we still don’t know
slides.text: Nobody knows how many expeditions crossed the Atlantic or how long the Vikings stayed. The researchers think their time there was fairly short, with a small cultural and ecological legacy. Plant remains at the site suggest they also explored lands further south than Newfoundland.

slides.question: What showed that Europeans, not local people, had cut the wood?
slides.explanation: Each piece carried cut marks from metal blades. The Indigenous people of the region did not produce metal, so the cuts point to the Norse.

source.label: University of Groningen: Europeans in the Americas 1000 years ago
